lesson.title: Check before you trust
lesson.subtitle: Why AI can sound sure — and still be wrong

video.title: Check before you trust
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Chat answers are shown as lines, never readable app names. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — Grade 8 science teacher (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Evening at Mr Okafor’s table: exercise books, a science textbook and a phone. On the phone, his question sits in a chat bubble; a long, neat answer appears below as lines, with one small book icon. Mr Okafor leans back, delighted, and gives a thumbs up.
scenes.animation: Answer lines type in fast, top to bottom; book icon pops (150 ms). Quick push-in on his smile.
scenes.narration: Two great facts and a book to cite — in ten seconds! Lesson planning done.
scenes.sound: Soft phone taps; light music bed starts.
scenes.vids: Phone: flat illustration, text shown as lines — no readable app name or logo. Mr Okafor: friendly Nigerian science teacher, ink outlines; keep his design the same across the unit.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the lesson title and a yellow ‘AI’ track chip with the spark icon. The small book icon from the answer drifts in and turns into a dashed outline.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up; book outline fades to dashes.
scenes.narration: But one fact is wrong. And the book doesn’t exist. Today: check before you trust.
scenes.vids: Use the Darsi title template (see brand kit). Keep the chip as icon + word.

scenes.visual: A chat bubble fills with words one at a time, shown as grey blocks. Above each gap, three word chips of different sizes hover; the biggest drops into place. Behind the bubble, a huge stack of page shapes. Small inset: the phone keyboard from Lesson 1 suggesting a word.
scenes.animation: Chips pop in (150 ms); the largest slides into the gap. Repeat three times, faster each time.
scenes.on_screen_text: One likely word at a time
scenes.narration: How can that happen? A chatbot writes one likely word at a time. It learned which words usually come next from huge amounts of text — like your phone keyboard, on a much bigger scale.
scenes.sound: Soft click as each word drops in.
scenes.vids: Build with Vids shapes: grey rounded blocks for words, no readable text inside. Keep chips large enough to read at 240p.

scenes.visual: Two jars on a shelf. The left jar (speech-bubble icon) is full of word shapes: how sentences sound. The right jar (check-and-cross icon) is empty: no true or false labels. A fact card with a calendar and a book has a blank; a word shape slides in and glows. It fits — but it’s a guess.
scenes.animation: Left jar fills; right jar stays empty. The word shape snaps into the blank with a glow (200 ms); a small question mark appears above it.
scenes.narration: But it learned how sentences sound, not which facts are true: its training text had no ‘true’ or ‘false’ labels. For a rare fact, like a date or a book title, it may guess — and the guess sounds just as sure. Many tests of chatbots even reward a guess over ‘I don’t know’.
scenes.sound: A soft ‘ding’ as the guess snaps in.
scenes.vids: Jars and cards as flat shapes. Put any jar labels in Vids text boxes, not in the image, so they can be translated.

scenes.visual: Definition card on white with the AI track chip. Three icons in a row: speech bubble (an answer) → sparkle (sounds sure) → cross in a circle (but false). Below them, three small ghost cards with dashed outlines: a fact, a quote mark and a book.
scenes.animation: Icons appear one by one, 300 ms apart, with arrows drawing between them. Ghost cards fade in last.
scenes.narration: This is called a hallucination: an answer that sounds sure but is false or made up — a fact, a quote, even a book. The AI isn’t lying on purpose. It’s predicting, and predictions can be wrong.
scenes.vids: Keep the card on screen for at least 6 seconds so teachers can read it in a second language.

scenes.visual: A simple courtroom: a judge’s bench, a gavel, two lawyers at a table with a stack of six case papers. The papers flicker and turn into dashed outlines. Then a world map fills with small dots while a counter climbs past 2,000.
scenes.animation: Papers fade to dashed outlines one by one (6 × 150 ms). Gavel taps once. Map dots pop in; counter ticks up.
scenes.narration: In 2023, US lawyers cited six court cases a chatbot had invented — and stood by them. One even asked the chatbot if a case was real — it said yes. They were fined five thousand dollars. By October 2026, over two thousand court decisions worldwide had found AI-made-up content.
scenes.sound: One gavel tap; soft ticking for the counter.
scenes.vids: Neutral courtroom illustration: no flags, logos or likenesses of real people. The counter is a Vids text box.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor holds up his phone with the confident answer, grinning. Two big answer cards drop in beside him: ‘Yes — it sounds sure’ and ‘Not necessarily — check’.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! My chatbot sounded very sure. Its answer is probably right… isn’t it?
scenes.sound: Two gentle ‘pop’ sounds for the cards.
scenes.vids: The app pauses here (diamond marker). For the MP4 shared outside the app, hold this frame for 3 seconds with a small countdown ring.

scenes.visual: The ‘Not necessarily — check’ card gets a blue check badge. A magnifying glass slides over Mr Okafor’s phone. Beside it, a medical student reads AI advice on a screen with a small warning triangle; the triangle blinks, and nothing changes.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms). Quick 0.8 s confetti of three shapes in kola, sunbird and ink. Warning triangle blinks once.
scenes.narration: Not necessarily. Sounding sure isn’t being right — chatbot makers warn about this themselves. But in a 2026 trial, a warning label didn’t change how much medical students relied on AI. So let’s build a habit.
scenes.vids: Use blue for correct (never green) and always pair it with the check icon.

scenes.visual: Three cards slide in, as in the board diagram. Ask (speech bubble): Mr Okafor types; his class list, with a lock, stays off to the side. Check (magnifying glass): an atlas opens at Lake Victoria, three country outlines pulse; an empty library shelf. Decide (hand, yellow): he ticks one fact, corrects one, crosses out the book.
scenes.animation: Cards slide in 300 ms apart. Atlas page flips; country outlines pulse once. Tick, pencil fix and cross appear in turn.
scenes.narration: Here’s the habit. Ask clearly — never put pupils’ names, marks, phone numbers or photos into an AI tool. Check important facts in a trusted source: Mr Okafor’s atlas confirms the Nile fact, but Lake Victoria is shared by three countries. And the book? He can’t find it anywhere. Then decide: keep, fix or drop.
scenes.sound: Page flip; soft tick, pencil scratch, cross.
scenes.vids: Mirror the lesson’s board diagram: same order, icons and colours (only ‘Decide’ in yellow). Map: simple outlines, no tiny place names.

scenes.visual: Three quick cards, about 6 seconds each: an investigator at a desk looks at a payment flagged on screen; a health worker holds a sample tube beside a chest X-ray with one highlighted spot; a family listens to an official flood warning on a radio, a river map with an alert badge behind them.
scenes.animation: Each card flips in from the right; a small hand icon lands on each to show a person decides.
scenes.narration: Experts do the same. A mobile money company in Kenya says investigators review what its fraud AI flags. AI that reads chest X-rays for TB only flags who might be ill — a lab test must confirm. One flood forecast service says its forecasts are for information only.
scenes.vids: Flat icons from the Darsi set on white cards. No company names, logos or real X-ray images; use a simple drawn chest outline.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma Haddad, one eyebrow raised and a half-smile, holds up two request cards: one with a quiz icon and a water drop, one with a class list showing name lines and marks.
scenes.animation: Salma slides in; cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Which request is safe to type into an AI tool?
scenes.vids: Second diamond marker — the app pauses for the question. In the MP4, hold for 3 seconds, then highlight the quiz card.

scenes.visual: The quiz card gets the check badge. The screen resolves into three summary cards in a row: speech bubble (Ask), magnifying glass (Check), hand (Decide) — the last one in yellow.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: The quiz — no pupils’ details. Remember: AI can be useful, but it predicts; it doesn’t check facts the way a careful person does. So ask clearly, check what matters, then decide. You’re the teacher; the AI is a tool.
scenes.vids: Hold the three cards for 5 seconds. Same icons and order as the board diagram.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor’s classroom. He reads from a slip of paper in a playful robot pose; pupils hold up one to five fingers to vote. A pupil points to a page in the textbook. The board shows three chalk boxes: speech bubble, magnifying glass, hand. End card: Darsi mark and ‘Next unit: How chatbots work’.
scenes.animation: Fingers pop up across the class; the textbook page highlights. End card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: read five statements in a robot voice — one is made up. Pupils vote for the fake and say how they’d check: textbook, teacher, library or an elder. End with Ask, Check, Decide.
scenes.sound: Music resolves; no end jingle longer than 1 s.
scenes.vids: Classroom: illustrated pupils in local school uniforms; avoid stereotyped imagery. End card from the Darsi template.

checkpoints.prompt: Mr Okafor’s chatbot sounded very sure. Is its answer probably right?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — sounding sure isn’t proof. Chatbots can sound confident even when a fact is wrong, so check what matters.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — chatbots can sound just as confident when they are wrong. Their makers warn about this, so check what matters.

checkpoints.prompt: Which request is safe to type into an AI tool?

options.text: Reports with pupils’ names and marks

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it asks clearly and shares no personal details. Pupils’ names and marks stay out of AI tools.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — names and marks are pupils’ personal details. Keep them out of AI tools, and ask for general help instead.

video.vids_prompt: Create a 3 minute 49 second animated explainer video for teachers titled “Check before you trust”. Style: flat, friendly illustration with bold ink outlines, light grey backgrounds, a tangerine (#ff6a2b) brand colour and a sunny yellow (#ffc53d) accent; no gradients or blur. Main character: Mr Okafor, a Grade 8 science teacher in Nigeria; cameo: Ms Salma Haddad, a maths teacher. Follow the attached script scene by scene: a chatbot gives a confident answer with a wrong fact and a book that doesn’t exist; chatbots write one likely word at a time; what a hallucination is; lawyers fined over invented court cases; two quiz pauses; the Ask, Check, Decide habit; people checking AI; end with a classroom game. Use the narration exactly as written, a warm, calm voice, and keep on-screen text to six words or fewer per scene.
